s1.title: Sentences: joining two full sentences
s1.big:
A full sentence has a who + a did and can stand alone.
Two full sentences need a strong joiner between them.
s1.defn: A full sentence (independent clause) has a subject (who) and a verb (did) and makes sense by itself. A strong joiner is the punctuation that can connect two full sentences: a period, a semicolon, or a comma + FANBOYS (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so).
s1.sat: the blank sits where two parts meet. Before you look at the choices, cover each side and ask: full or not full?
s1.hook: A semicolon is a period wearing a hat. A comma alone is a broken bridge: it can't hold two full sentences.
how: Cover the right side of the blank. Is the left side a full sentence?
Cover the left side. Is the right side a full sentence?
Both full → . or ; or , + FANBOYS. Only one full → a comma (or nothing).
s1.rem: Full + full needs a period, a semicolon, or a comma + FANBOYS. A comma alone is wrong (comma splice). Nothing at all is wrong (run-on).

ex.s: The volcano erupted in 1815[[.]] Crops failed across Europe the next year.
ex.why: Both sides are full sentences, so a period works.
parts: Crops failed across Europe the next year.
ex.trap: 1815, crops: Puts only a comma between two full sentences. The volcano erupted in 1815, crops failed… A comma alone can’t hold two full sentences. That is called a comma splice.

ex.s: The Mission 66 plan improved national parks[[;]] it rebuilt roads and visitor centers.
ex.why: Both sides are full. A semicolon = a period, so it works.
parts: The Mission 66 plan improved national parks
it rebuilt roads and visitor centers.
ex.trap: parks it: Puts nothing between two full sentences. The Mission 66 plan improved national parks it rebuilt roads… Two full sentences crashing together with no joiner is a run-on.

ex.s: The first trial looked promising[[, but]] the drug failed later.
ex.why: Full + full, joined by a comma plus “but.” That is a strong joiner.
ex.trap: promising but,: Puts the comma after “but.” The first trial looked promising but, the drug failed. The comma always goes before the FANBOYS word, never after.

ex.s: The trial looked promising[[; however,]] the drug failed.
ex.why: “However” is not a FANBOYS word, so it can’t join with just commas. Semicolon before, comma after.
ex.trap: , however,: Puts only commas around “however.” The trial looked promising, however, the drug failed. That is still a comma splice. “However” is not a FANBOYS word.

ex.s: The poet was nervous[[, but]] her reading went well.
ex.why: Comma + but is already a strong joiner. That is enough.
ex.trap: ; but: Puts a semicolon and “but.” The poet was nervous; but her reading went well. The semicolon already joins. Adding “but” doubles up.

ex.s: The plan was simple[[:]] the team would map the cave first.
ex.why: Sentence 2 tells you what the simple plan was. A colon introduces an explanation.
parts: the team would map the cave first.
ex.trap: The plan: was: Puts a colon after an unfinished thought. The plan: was to map the cave first. A colon needs a full sentence before it. “The plan” is not full.

ex.s: While one requires oxygen and one does not[[,]] aerobic and anaerobic respiration are both forms of cellular respiration.
ex.why: The left side starts with “while,” so it can’t stand alone. Starter first → one comma. (Real College Board question.)
parts: While one requires oxygen and one does not
aerobic and anaerobic respiration are both forms…
ex.trap: not. Aerobic: Puts a period after the starter part. While one requires oxygen and one does not. That leaves “While one requires oxygen…” alone as a fragment. It can’t stand alone.

ex.s: The river finally rose[[ ]]after the drought ended.
ex.why: Only the left side is full. Starter second → no punctuation.
ex.trap: rose; after: Puts a semicolon before the starter part. The river finally rose; after the drought ended. A semicolon needs a full sentence on both sides. “after the drought ended” is not full.

ex.s: The chemist heated the sample[[ and]] recorded the color change.
ex.why: The right side has no who of its own, so it is not full. No comma before “and.”
ex.trap: sample, and: Puts a comma before “and.” The chemist heated the sample, and recorded the color change. Comma + and is only for joining two full sentences. “recorded the color change” has no who.

ex.s: Historians divide Egyptian history into three periods[[:]] the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms.
ex.why: Full sentence first, then a list → colon. (Based on a real College Board question.)
parts: Historians divide Egyptian history into three periods
the Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms.
ex.trap: periods. The: Puts a period before the list. into three periods. The Old, Middle, and New Kingdoms. The list can’t stand alone as a sentence. It becomes a fragment.

s2.title: No wall: no punctuation between words that belong together
s2.big:
Some words belong together.
Never put any punctuation between them.
s2.defn: Punctuation creates a pause or a break. Words that are one unit, like a who and its did, must not be split by a comma, colon, semicolon, or dash.
s2.sat: if the choices only differ by a comma, colon, or nothing, ask: do the words on each side belong together? If yes, pick no punctuation.
s2.hook: Words that belong together are holding hands: never put a wall between them.
how: Look at the words on each side of the blank.
Do they belong together (who+did, did+what, about+its words, title+name)?
If yes, no punctuation.
s2.rem: Keep words that belong together: who + did, did + what, a little word + its words, a title + the name. Never put a comma, colon or semicolon between them.

ex.s: The scientists who studied the reef[[ ]]published their results.
ex.why: However long the who is, it stays glued to its did.
parts: The scientists who studied the reef
ex.trap: reef, published: Puts a comma between the who and the did. The scientists who studied the reef, published their results. It splits the subject from its verb. Nothing is extra here.

ex.s: The two nations signed[[ ]]the treaty in 1848.
ex.why: “Signed” needs its object right after it.
ex.trap: signed: the treaty: Puts a colon after the verb. The two nations signed: the treaty. A colon needs a full sentence before it. “The two nations signed” is not finished.

ex.s: String theory faces questions about[[ ]]whether its ideas can be tested.
ex.why: “About” and what it is about are one unit. (Your practice test Q15.)
parts: whether its ideas can be tested.
ex.trap: questions: about: Puts a colon before “about.” String theory faces questions: about whether… It walls off “about” from the noun it describes.

ex.s: Entomologist Heather Grab[[ ]]found that clearing wild growth reduced bee species.
ex.why: Two no-wall rules: title + name, and who + did. (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: Entomologist, Heather Grab,: Puts commas around the name. Entomologist, Heather Grab, found… Lift out “Heather Grab” and you get “Entomologist found,” which breaks. The name is needed, not extra.

ex.s: The study found[[ ]]that sleep improves reaction time.
ex.why: The “that” part is the thing found. It belongs to the verb.
ex.trap: found, that: Puts a comma before “that.” The study found, that sleep improves… It walls off the verb from what it found.

ex.s: writers such as[[ ]]Zora Neale Hurston and Langston Hughes
ex.why: “Such as” already introduces the list.
parts: Zora Neale Hurston and Langston Hughes
ex.trap: such as:: Adds a colon after “such as.” writers such as: Zora Neale Hurston… Doubling up. “Such as” does the colon’s job already.

ex.s: Students who miss the lab[[ ]]must make it up.
ex.why: Not all students make it up, only those who miss. The who-part is needed, so no commas.
ex.trap: Students, who miss the lab,: Puts commas around the who-part. Students, who miss the lab, must make it up. Commas make it extra, which would mean all students must make it up. Wrong meaning.

s3.title: Apostrophes and pronouns
s3.big:
An apostrophe shows ownership.
It goes on the owner, never on the thing owned.
s3.defn: A possessive shows that something belongs to someone. One owner → ’s. More than one owner ending in s → s’. Pronouns (its, their, whose) never use an apostrophe to own: it’s = it is, they’re = they are.
s3.sat: first ask “is the next word owned?” Then count the owners. For pronouns, read it as “it is” or “they are” to test.
s3.hook: Say it out loud: if "it is" or "they are" sounds wrong, the apostrophe is wrong.
how: Find the word right after the blank. Is it owned?
Count the owners: one or more than one?
Pronoun? Read "it is / they are" in its place to test.
s3.rem: One owner: scientist's. Many owners: scientists'. Just many: scientists. Its owns; it's = it is. Never put the apostrophe on the thing owned. Never use it's or they're to show owning.

ex.s: The [[author’s]] political writings sparked a revolution.
ex.why: One author owns the writings → author’s. (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: authors’ … writings’: Puts apostrophes on both words. the authors’ political writings’ There is only one author, and the writings own nothing.

ex.s: Rice and tomatoes: the two [[plants’]] genetic profiles share 68 gene families.
ex.why: Two plants own the profiles → plants’. (Your practice test Q16.)
ex.trap: plants genetic profiles’: Puts the apostrophe on the thing owned. the two plants genetic profiles’ The profiles don’t own anything. The plants do.

ex.t: Plural that doesn’t end in s
ex.s: The [[children’s]] books were donated.
ex.why: “Children” is already plural, so add ’s.
ex.trap: childrens’: Adds s then apostrophe. the childrens’ books “Childrens” is not a word.

ex.s: The [[scientists]] collected samples.
ex.why: The next word is an action, not something owned → no apostrophe.
ex.trap: scientist’s: Adds an apostrophe to a plain plural. The scientist’s collected samples. Nothing belongs to the scientists here.

ex.s: A butterfly flapping [[its wings]] might start a storm.
ex.why: “Flapping it is wings” fails, so its. (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: it’s wings: Uses it’s (it is). flapping it is wings Nonsense. It’s only ever means “it is.”

ex.s: Two paintings are similar in [[their]] use of large canvases.
ex.why: Two paintings own the use → their. (Your practice test Q17.)
ex.trap: they’re: Uses they’re (they are). similar in they are use Nonsense. Nothing is “they are” here.

ex.t: Count the owners: one or many
ex.s: There were two calendars, and [[their]] dates rarely aligned.
ex.why: Two calendars → their. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q17.)
ex.trap: its: Uses the one-owner word. two calendars, and its dates “Its” is for one owner. There are two calendars.

ex.s: The company raised [[its]] prices.
ex.why: A group word counts as one.
ex.trap: their: Uses the many-owner word. The company raised their prices. One company → its.

ex.s: the author [[whose]] novel won the prize
ex.why: “The author who is novel” fails → whose.
ex.trap: who’s: Uses who’s (who is). the author who is novel Nonsense.

s4.title: Pairs: matching marks around extra info
s4.big:
Extra information can be lifted out of a sentence.
It needs a matching pair of marks around it.
s4.defn: Extra information (a nonessential element) adds detail, but the sentence still works without it. It gets two matching marks: two commas, two dashes, or two parentheses. Never mix them, and never use just one.
s4.sat: find the mark that is already there first. The blank must match it. Then do the lift-out test: cover the extra info. Does the sentence still work?
how: Find the extra info (a name, a description, a "who/which" part).
Lift it out. Does the sentence still work?
Yes → match the mark that opens it.
s4.rem: Lift out the extra info. If the sentence still works, put matching marks on both sides. Never one sock, never mixed socks.

ex.s: A rare carbon isotope[[,]] carbon-13 (13C)[[,]] builds up in bears that eat human food.
ex.why: Lift out “carbon-13 (13C)” and the sentence still works. Comma opened it, so a comma closes it. (Based on a real College Board question.)
ex.trap: carbon-13 (13C): Leaves out the closing comma. a rare carbon isotope, carbon-13 (13C) due to… One sock. The extra info was opened and never closed.

ex.s: The plant’s chloroplasts[[—]]the organs that make energy from light[[—]]reshuffled to collect more light.
ex.why: The closing dash is already there, so the opening mark must be a dash too. (Based on a real College Board question.)
parts: the organs that make energy from light
ex.trap: chloroplasts,: Opens with a comma, closes with a dash. chloroplasts, the organs… light—reshuffled Mixed socks. The marks must match.

ex.s: The observatory [[(]]built in 1897[[)]] houses a huge telescope.
ex.why: Lift out “built in 1897”: “The observatory houses a huge telescope.” Still works.
ex.trap: 1897),: Adds a comma after the closing parenthesis. The observatory (built in 1897), houses… That comma walls off the who (observatory) from its did (houses).

ex.s: A self-taught fossil hunter[[,]] Mary Anning made major discoveries.
ex.why: The sentence starts with the extra info, so there is nothing to open. One comma closes it.
ex.trap: hunter Mary: Leaves out the comma. A self-taught fossil hunter Mary Anning made… Nothing separates the description from the sentence.

ex.s: The discovery was made by Mary Anning[[,]] a self-taught fossil hunter.
ex.why: The period at the end does the closing job.
parts: The discovery was made by Mary Anning
ex.trap: Anning a self-taught: Leaves out the comma. made by Mary Anning a self-taught fossil hunter. The description runs straight into the name.

ex.s: The Library of Congress[[,]] which was founded in 1800[[,]] holds millions of books.
ex.why: Which-parts add extra detail. Lift it out and the sentence still works.
ex.trap: 1800 holds: Leaves out the closing comma. …which was founded in 1800 holds millions… One sock: it was opened and not closed.

ex.s: The novel was written by author[[ ]]Toni Morrison.
ex.why: Lift out the name: “written by author.” That breaks, so the name is needed.
ex.trap: author, Toni Morrison,: Puts commas around the name. written by author, Toni Morrison, The name is not extra. Without it the sentence breaks.

s5.title: Subject X-ray and verb form
s5.big:
The verb must match the real who.
One thing → is / has / -s. Many → are / have / no -s.
s5.defn: Subject-verb agreement means a singular subject takes a singular verb (is, has, runs) and a plural subject takes a plural verb (are, have, run). Words between the subject and verb do not change it. A sentence also needs one main verb per who: if the main verb is already there, a describing blank takes -ing.
s5.sat: if the choices are different forms of the same verb, X-ray the sentence: cross out the middle, find the who, count it.
s5.hook: X-ray the sentence: see through the extra words to find the who.
how: Cross out the middle stuff.
Find the who. One or many?
Already have a main did? Then the blank is -ing, not a 2nd verb.
s5.rem: Cross out the middle, find the who, match one or many. Don't match the verb to the noun right before it. Don't add a 2nd main verb: use -ing.

ex.s: The collection of rare letters [[is]] kept in a vault.
ex.why: The collection (one) is kept. The letters are not the who.
ex.trap: are: Matches the verb to “letters.” The collection of rare letters are kept… “Letters” is inside the of-phrase. The who is “collection.”

ex.t: Dashes or commas in the middle
ex.s: Throat singing—a tradition with two performers—[[has found]] an advocate.
ex.why: X-ray: “Throat singing has found.” (Your practice test Q18.)
ex.trap: find: Uses a plural verb. Throat singing… find an advocate Throat singing is one thing. “Find” is for many.

ex.s: The botanist and the chemist [[are]] on the panel.
ex.why: Two people → are.
ex.trap: is: Uses a singular verb. The botanist and the chemist is… A + B = two.

ex.s: The director, along with her assistants, [[is]] arriving.
ex.why: Only the director is the who.
ex.trap: are: Matches “assistants.” The director, along with her assistants, are… “Along with” is extra. The who is one director.

ex.s: Each of the samples [[has]] a label.
ex.why: “Each” always means one.
ex.trap: have: Matches “samples.” Each of the samples have… “Samples” is in the of-phrase. Each = one.

ex.s: There [[are]] three reasons.
ex.why: Flip it: “three reasons are.”
ex.trap: is: Uses singular. There is three reasons. The who is three reasons, which is many.

ex.s: Lindqvist detected a profile closely [[matching]] nearby communities.
ex.why: “Detected” is the main verb. The blank describes the profile → -ing. (Your practice test Q20.)
ex.trap: matches: Adds a second main verb. Lindqvist detected a profile closely matches… There is no who for “matches.” One main verb per who.

ex.t: A “that” part needs a real verb
ex.s: columnar jointing, a pattern of fracturing that [[results]] in long prisms
ex.why: The that-part needs its own real verb. Pattern is one → results. (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: resulting: Uses -ing. a pattern that resulting in prisms “That resulting” has no real verb.

ex.s: Richard Serra[[, intending]] his art to make people aware of space, builds huge steel sculptures.
ex.why: “Builds” is the main verb, so the extra part is -ing, with a comma on each side. (Based on a real College Board question.)
ex.trap: Serra intends: Adds a second main verb. Richard Serra intends his art to…, builds… Now Serra has two main verbs and the comma has no partner.

s6.title: CARE: how do the two sentences connect?
s6.big:
A transition is a bridge word between two sentences.
It tells you how sentence 2 connects to sentence 1.
s6.defn: A transition is a linking word or phrase (however, therefore, for example) that tells the reader how one sentence connects to the next.
s6.sat: the transition is a blank, and all 4 choices are transition words. Your job is to decide how the sentences connect first, then pick the word.
s6.hook: Do you CARE how they connect? Decide before you look.
how: Cover the choices.
Say C, A, R or E out loud.
Pick from that group only. Cross out the others.
s6.rem: Decide C, A, R or E before you look at the choices. Don't pick a word from the wrong group just because it sounds smart.

ex.s: The first trial looked promising. [[However,]] the drug failed in the larger study.
ex.why: Good news, then bad news. Sentence 2 goes the opposite way, so it is Contrast.
parts: the drug failed in the larger study.
ex.trap: Therefore: “Therefore” is a R · RESULT word. It means: because of that; so. The first trial looked promising, so the drug failed. A good trial does not cause a drug to fail. Sentence 1 did not make sentence 2 happen.

ex.s: Bou could photograph rare birds. [[Instead,]] he tracks the flight paths of common birds.
ex.why: He picks something different from what sentence 1 offered. Swapping one thing for another is Contrast.
parts: he tracks the flight paths of common birds.
ex.trap: Similarly: “Similarly” is a A · ADD word. It means: in the same way; likewise. Bou could photograph rare birds. In the same way, he tracks common birds. Rare and common birds are a different choice. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q22.)

ex.s: “Third spaces” have sparked enormous new interest. [[Nonetheless,]] the idea dates back to 1989.
ex.why: S1 makes it sound new; S2 says it is not new. Pushing back is Contrast.
parts: “Third spaces” have sparked enormous new interest.
ex.trap: Furthermore: “Furthermore” is a A · ADD word. It means: and also; one more point on the same side. Third spaces sparked new interest. And also, the idea dates back to 1989. S2 does not add another reason it is new. It pushes against S1. (Your practice test Q25.)

ex.s: The new plan has worked well. [[Granted,]] it is expensive.
ex.why: A plus, then a minus. Admitting the other side is Contrast.
parts: The new plan has worked well.
ex.trap: Therefore: “Therefore” is a R · RESULT word. It means: because of that; so. The plan has worked well, so it is expensive. Working well does not cause a plan to cost a lot.

ex.s: Most known planets orbit stars like our Sun. In 2014, [[however,]] researchers found a planet orbiting a far hotter star.
ex.why: S2 breaks the pattern from S1, so it is Contrast. (Based on a real College Board question.)
parts: Most known planets orbit stars like our Sun.
researchers found a planet orbiting a far hotter star.
ex.trap: likewise: “likewise” is a A · ADD word. It means: in the same way. Most planets orbit Sun-like stars. In the same way, one orbits a far hotter star. A hotter star is not the same as a Sun-like star.

ex.s: Bees pollinate many crops. [[Moreover,]] they produce honey and wax.
ex.why: Two good things in a row. No turn, just one more, so it is Add.
ex.trap: However: “However” is a C · CONTRAST word. It means: but; going the opposite way. Bees pollinate many crops, but they produce honey and wax. Both sentences are good things. Nothing goes the opposite way.

ex.s: In her poems, Rita Dove sets Thomas’s life against the Great Migration. [[Similarly,]] she sets Beulah’s life against the Civil Rights Movement.
ex.why: Two characters, each set against history. Alike is Add. (Based on a real College Board question.)
ex.trap: Thus: “Thus” is a R · RESULT word. It means: because of that; so. Dove sets Thomas’s life against history, so she sets Beulah’s against history. The first did not cause the second. They are just alike.

ex.s: Shōen mixed new subjects with old techniques. [[Indeed,]] her works show the contrasts of her era.
ex.why: S2 says “yes, and here is the proof.” Confirming is Add.
parts: Shōen mixed new subjects with old techniques.
her works show the contrasts of her era.
ex.trap: In addition: “In addition” is a A · ADD word. It means: plus one new, separate fact. Shōen mixed old and new. Plus a separate fact: her works show her era’s contrasts. S2 is not a separate fact. It proves S1, so “Indeed” fits better. (Your practice test Q26.)

ex.s: The experiment was flawless. [[That is,]] every measurement matched the prediction.
ex.why: Same idea, said a clearer way. Restating is Add.
ex.trap: For example: “For example” is a E · EXAMPLE word. It means: here is one case of it. The experiment was flawless. One case of that: every measurement matched. “Every measurement matched” is not one case. It is the same idea said more clearly.

ex.s: The lead scientist fell ill. [[As a result,]] the study was delayed by six months.
ex.why: Test it: “She fell ill, so the study was delayed.” That makes sense, so it is Result.
parts: the study was delayed by six months.
ex.trap: For example: “For example” is a E · EXAMPLE word. It means: here is one case of it. The lead scientist fell ill. One case of that: the study was delayed. The delay is not one case of being ill. It is what the illness caused.

ex.t: A finding leads to a conclusion
ex.s: Honeybees recognized human faces in lab tests. [[Therefore,]] some scientists now think insect memory is more complex than once believed.
ex.why: The test led to the new belief. Because of = Result.
parts: Honeybees recognized human faces in lab tests.
scientists now think insect memory is complex.
ex.trap: However: “However” is a C · CONTRAST word. It means: but; going the opposite way. Honeybees recognized faces, but scientists think insect memory is complex. The conclusion agrees with the finding. Nothing goes the opposite way.

ex.s: Sleeping brains show contradictory patterns. [[For example,]] cells that respond to sound turn on while others stay off.
ex.why: S1 is the big idea. S2 is one specific case of it. Zooming in is Example.
parts: sound cells turn on while others stay off.
ex.trap: In general: “In general” is a ZOOM-OUT (opposite of Example) word. It means: speaking broadly; the big picture. Sleeping brains show contradictory patterns. Speaking broadly, sound cells turn on… S2 is one specific case, not the big picture. (Your practice test Q21.)

ex.s: Many great inventions began as accidents. [[For instance,]] penicillin was discovered when mold grew on a forgotten lab dish.
ex.why: Penicillin is one case of an accidental invention, so it is Example.
parts: Many great inventions began as accidents.
ex.trap: Therefore: “Therefore” is a R · RESULT word. It means: because of that; so. Many inventions began as accidents, so penicillin was discovered. Other inventions did not cause the mold to grow.

ex.s: The soldiers’ work on the Alaska Highway was overlooked for decades. [[Then,]] in 2017, lawmakers declared a day to honor them.
ex.why: Decades of nothing, and then 2017. Events in order are Time. (Based on a real College Board question.)
ex.trap: For example: “For example” is a E · EXAMPLE word. It means: here is one case of it. The work was overlooked. One case of that: in 2017 lawmakers honored them. Being honored is not a case of being overlooked. It is the opposite, and it came later.

r1.title: Words in context
r1.big:
The right word is the one the text’s clue points to.
Say your own simple word first, then find the match.
r1.defn: A words-in-context question asks which word best fits a blank (or what a word means) in this text. The answer is decided by a clue in the text, not by which word sounds smartest.
r1.sat: cover the 4 choices. Find the clue, put your own simple word in the blank, then pick the choice closest to your word.
r1.hook: Fill the blank with your word first, then shop for a match.
how: Cover the choices.
Find the clue and say your own word.
Match. Cross out choices that mean something else.
r1.rem: Cover the choices, find the clue, say your own word, pick the closest match. Don't pick a word just because it sounds advanced.

ex.s: Foreign problems led to [[unrest]] within Russia. For instance, protests broke out.
ex.why: Protests are a kind of trouble → unrest. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q2.)
ex.trap: explanations: Wrong meaning Foreign problems led to explanations… For instance, protests broke out. Protests are not explanations.

ex.s: The play served a [[twofold]] purpose: it criticized one thing and showed an alternative.
ex.why: Two jobs → twofold. (Your practice test Q4.)
ex.trap: external: Sounds smart, wrong meaning served an external purpose Nothing about “outside.” The clue is “two jobs.”

ex.s: Faulkner’s novels [[exhibited]] world-building ambitions long before fantasy made it common.
ex.why: The novels showed those ambitions → exhibited. (Your practice test Q3.)
ex.trap: overcame: Wrong meaning Faulkner’s novels overcame world-building ambitions You don’t “overcome” your own ambitions. The clue says they had them.

ex.s: Whereas some languages show [[decoupling]] of words for one object, Pacific languages show the opposite: similarity.
ex.why: The opposite of similarity is separation → decoupling. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q5.)
ex.trap: renderings: Off-topic word some languages show renderings Renderings are versions or translations, not the opposite of similarity.

ex.s: Unlike her outspoken colleagues, the physicist was [[reserved]], rarely speaking to reporters.
ex.why: Opposite of outspoken + rarely speaks → quiet → reserved.
ex.trap: boastful: Same as the clue, not the opposite Unlike her outspoken colleagues, she was boastful Boastful matches outspoken. “Unlike” needs the opposite.

ex.s: The new evidence [[undermined]] the old theory; researchers could no longer accept it.
ex.why: They stopped accepting it, so the evidence weakened it → undermined.
ex.trap: confirmed: Opposite meaning The new evidence confirmed the theory; researchers could no longer accept it. If it confirmed the theory, they would accept it more, not less.

ex.s: The architect’s plan was [[sound]]: every part had been tested.
ex.why: Here “sound” means solid, sensible, not a noise.
ex.trap: noisy: Most common meaning, wrong here The plan was noisy: every part had been tested. A plan can’t be noisy. Use the meaning the clue supports.

r2.title: Main idea
r2.big:
The main idea covers the whole text,
not just one detail.
r2.defn: The main idea (central idea) is the most important point the whole text makes. Every sentence supports it. A detail is just one piece.
r2.sat: the main idea is often after the turn (however, but, a new study) or in the last sentence. Say it in 5 words before you look.
r2.hook: Main idea = the headline, not one detail from the article.
how: Read the whole text.
Say the point in 5 words.
Cross out: too small, too extreme, never said.
r2.rem: Say the point of the whole text in 5 words. Cross out: too small, too extreme, never said.

ex.s: People thought the cave’s humming was random. A study found wind through one opening causes it.
ex.why: The main idea is what the study found.
ex.trap: Visitors have always feared the cave.: Never said Does the text mention fear? No. It’s not in the text at all.

ex.t: “Some think X. However, Y argues Z.”
ex.s: Earlier historians saw the herbal as a simple guide. However, Holt sees it as both practical and moral.
ex.why: The author sets up the old view to knock it down. The point is Holt’s view.
ex.trap: Earlier historians were right.: Picks the setup, not the point Does the text agree with the earlier view? No. “However” turns away from it.

ex.s: The first gummy bears looked very different. Riegel’s changes helped them [[evolve]] into today’s form.
ex.why: Before → after = change. (Your practice test Q7.)
ex.trap: Early gummy bears would be unrecognizable today.: Too extreme Does it say “unrecognizable”? It says “different,” not unrecognizable.

ex.s: Monarchs fly 3,000 miles each fall. No single butterfly makes the round trip; it takes several generations.
ex.why: The surprising whole: the journey spans generations.
ex.trap: Each monarch flies 3,000 miles twice.: Contradicts the text Does one butterfly make the round trip? The text says no single butterfly does.

r3.title: Inferences: finish the thought
r3.big:
An inference is the ending the text’s facts prove.
No outside ideas. No going further than the facts.
r3.defn: An inference question gives you a text that stops with a blank. The right answer is the most logical conclusion from the facts given, and nothing more.
r3.sat: underline the facts. Ask: what do these facts prove? Cross out anything outside the text or bigger than the facts.
r3.hook: Be a judge: only rule on what the evidence shows.
how: Underline the facts.
Read the setup word (thus, proves).
Pick the ending that follows directly. Nothing extra.
r3.rem: Pick only what the facts prove. No outside ideas, no going further, no flipping the facts.

ex.s: Plants with the fungus had fewer wilted leaves in a dry month. This suggests that [[the fungus may help plants in dry conditions]].
ex.why: Fewer wilted leaves during dryness → it may help with dryness.
ex.trap: the fungus makes plants grow taller.: Outside the text Does the text mention height? No. That idea comes from outside the text.

ex.s: Plants with the fungus had [[fewer wilted leaves]].
ex.why: The facts are about wilted leaves only.
ex.trap: plants with the fungus produce twice as many tomatoes.: Goes too far Does the text measure tomatoes? No. It only measured leaves.

ex.s: They turned light into light 7 times higher in frequency. This proves that [[low-frequency light can become much higher-frequency light]].
ex.why: The ending matches the experiment. (Your practice test Q12.)
ex.trap: High-frequency light improves the material.: Backwards Which light was turned into which? Low became high, not the reverse.

ex.s: No Roman writings mention the objects. Finding [[such writings]] could solve the mystery.
ex.why: The missing piece is writings, so finding writings would help.
ex.trap: finding more objects: Doesn’t fix the gap Would more objects explain them? More objects don’t give the missing written explanation.

r4.title: Evidence: support, weaken, illustrate
r4.big:
Evidence must test the claim itself.
Support shows it is true. Weaken shows the opposite.
r4.defn: A claim is what someone says is true. Evidence is a finding or quotation that makes the claim more believable (supports it), less believable (weakens it), or shows it in action (illustrates it).
r4.sat: say the claim in 5 words. Read the question’s verb: support, weaken, or illustrate. The answer must mention both parts of the claim.
r4.hook: Find the exact claim being tested, then check the evidence for it.
how: Underline the claim. Say it in 5 words.
Support → shows it. Weaken → shows the opposite.
Cross out choices that only share the topic.
r4.rem: Say the claim in 5 words. Support = shows it; weaken = shows the opposite. Choices that only share the topic are traps.

ex.s: Claim: more sleep → fewer errors. [[9-hour sleepers made the fewest errors.]]
ex.why: It tests sleep and errors together.
ex.trap: Most students sleep 7 hours.: Only one part Does it mention errors? It doesn’t test the claim. It only describes sleep.

ex.s: Claim: more sleep → fewer errors. [[9-hour sleepers made as many errors as 6-hour sleepers.]]
ex.why: More sleep, same errors: the opposite of the claim.
ex.trap: 9-hour sleepers made the fewest errors.: Supports instead of weakens Does this go against the claim? No, it agrees with it.

ex.s: Claim: Nubia took on Egyptian customs when Nubia was weak. [[A powerful Nubian army still absorbed Egyptian customs.]]
ex.why: If strong Nubia also took on customs, weakness wasn’t the reason. (Your practice test Q11.)
ex.trap: Assyrian customs mixed in.: Off the claim Does it test weak vs. strong? No. It’s about a different culture.

ex.s: Claim: the novelist used humor to soften harsh events. [[“As the flood took the barn, Aunt Ruth complained only that the cows left without saying goodbye.”]]
ex.why: A harsh event + a joke about it = the claim in action.
ex.trap: “The flood swept away the barn and crops.”: Only one part Is there humor? Harsh, but no joke. It shows only half the claim.

ex.s: Claim: users work to restore the default. [[“I always return to the original color scheme.”]]
ex.why: Returning to the original = restoring the default. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q13.)
ex.trap: “Color schemes don’t matter to me.”: Opposite Does this person restore anything? No. It shows the opposite attitude.

ex.s: Claim: rainfall affects tree growth. [[Trees in the wettest region grew the most.]]
ex.why: It passes both checks.
ex.trap: Region C had the most trees.: True but off topic Is it about growth and rain? Number of trees is not growth.

r5.title: Purpose, structure, and two texts
r5.big:
Purpose = why the author wrote it.
Say it as a verb: to challenge, to explain, to compare.
r5.defn: A purpose question asks what the whole text (or one sentence) does. A structure question asks how the parts are arranged. A two-text question asks how Text 2 responds to Text 1.
r5.sat: write the verb before you look: challenge, explain, compare, describe, argue. Then match the whole text, not one part.
r5.hook: Purpose = why the author wrote it, not one fact inside it.
how: Say what the text does with a verb.
Check that it fits the whole text.
Two texts: T1 point → T2 agrees / disagrees / adds.
r5.rem: Purpose: a verb for the whole text. Two texts: T1 point, then agrees, disagrees or adds. Don't pick a choice about one sentence only.

ex.s: Many think deserts are lifeless. In fact, the Sonoran holds 3,500 plant species. [[To challenge a common view by showing variety.]]
ex.why: Belief + pushback = challenge.
ex.trap: To explain how cacti store water.: Never said Does the text talk about water storage? No. It’s not in the text.

ex.s: Carlyle said great individuals shape history; Spencer said society does. [[It sets up two opposing views explained later.]]
ex.why: Two opposite theories = contrasting viewpoints. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q6.)
ex.trap: It describes two theories that both rely on great individuals.: Misreads the text Do both rely on individuals? No. They are opposites.

ex.s: Text 1: children learn a language fastest by speaking daily. Text 2: daily speaking matters, but children first need weeks of listening. [[It accepts Text 1’s point but adds a condition.]]
ex.why: Agrees (speaking matters) + adds (listen first).
ex.trap: It completely rejects Text 1.: Too extreme Does Text 2 disagree with everything? No. It agrees daily speaking matters.

ex.s: Text 1: one microbe survives extreme heat. Text 2: another microbe resists radiation the same way. [[Text 2 extends Text 1 with a comparable strategy.]]
ex.why: Text 2 adds a similar case. (Your practice test, Module 2 Q8.)
ex.trap: The same environments harm the second microbe.: Never said Does Text 2 say it is harmed? No. It says it resists.

r6.title: Notes questions: do exactly the goal
r6.big:
A notes question gives you a goal.
The right answer does exactly that goal, and every other choice does something else.
r6.defn: In a rhetorical synthesis question, a student wrote bullet-point notes. You pick the sentence that uses the notes to meet a specific goal. All 4 choices are true; only one meets the goal.
r6.sat: skip the notes at first. Read the question, underline the goal, then check each choice: does it do that goal?
r6.hook: Answer the goal that was asked. A different true sentence is still the wrong answer.
how: Read the question. Underline the goal words.
Skip the notes at first.
Pick the choice that does every part of the goal.
r6.rem: Underline the goal, then pick the choice that does exactly that goal. A true fact that misses the goal is wrong.

ex.s: Goal: emphasize the library’s age. [[Founded in 1800, it is the oldest federal cultural institution.]]
ex.why: Every word is about age.
ex.trap: It holds more than 170 million items.: True but wrong goal Is it about age? No. It’s about size.

ex.s: Goal: explain the study’s outcome. [[Researchers arrived at a treatment that could restore smell.]]
ex.why: It gives the result. (Your practice test Q26.)
ex.trap: Researchers turned to gene therapy.: No outcome Does it say what happened? It only says what they tried.

ex.s: Goal: specify the number of faces. [[A regular octahedron has eight triangular faces.]]
ex.why: It gives the exact number. (Your Nov 8 miss.)
ex.trap: It has fewer faces than a dodecahedron.: No number Is there a number? Fewer than is a comparison, not a number.

ex.s: Goal: emphasize a similarity. [[Like bats, dolphins find food by using echoes.]]
ex.why: “Like” shows they are similar.
ex.trap: Bats fly; dolphins swim.: Difference Does it show they are alike? It shows how they differ.

ex.s: Goal: emphasize a difference. [[Venus reaches about 465°C, while Earth averages about 15°C.]]
ex.why: “While” compares two different numbers.
ex.trap: Venus is the hottest planet.: Only one thing Does it compare two things? It mentions only Venus.

ex.s: Goal: introduce Mary Anning to a new audience. [[Mary Anning, a self-taught English fossil hunter, found the first ichthyosaur skeleton.]]
ex.why: A new reader needs to know who she is.
ex.trap: Mary Anning found the first ichthyosaur skeleton.: No introduction Would a stranger know who she is? No. It assumes you already know her.

m1.title: Define FIND
m1.big:
Before you solve, write FIND: with the exact thing the question asks for.
Stop when you reach it.
m1.defn: The FIND is the exact quantity the question asks for. The SAT often asks for something one step past x: x − 5, 2x, the diameter, the number that did NOT pass.
m1.sat: answer choices almost always include x itself as a trap. Read the last line twice.
m1.hook: Know where you are going before you start driving.
how: Read the last line. Write FIND: .
Solve.
Before clicking: does my answer match the FIND?
m1.rem: Write FIND: first, and stop when you reach it. Don't solve for x when they ask for something else.

ex.t: Asks for an expression, not x
ex.s: If 3x + 2 = 29, what is x − 5?
ex.why: The question asked for x − 5, not x.
ex.trap: 9: Stopped at x. 9 is x. The FIND is x − 5. It answers a different question.

ex.s: If x ÷ 4 = 3, what is 2x?
ex.why: Double x once you have it.
ex.trap: 12: Stopped at x. x = 12, but the FIND is 2x. One step short.

ex.s: A circle has area 49π. What is its diameter?
ex.why: Area gives the radius. The question wants the diameter.
ex.trap: 7: Gave the radius. r = 7, d = 14. Radius is half the diameter.

ex.s: 1,200 students took a test and 92% passed. How many did NOT pass?
ex.why: Passed is a step. The FIND is the rest.
ex.trap: 1,104: Gave the number who passed. 1,104 passed; the question asks who did not. It answers the opposite question.

ex.s: The line y = 3x + c passes through (2, 11). What is c?
ex.why: Plug the point in and solve for c.
ex.trap: 11: Gave the y-value. Check: y = 3x + 11 at x = 2 gives 17, not 11. 11 is y, not c.

m2.title: Read the trap words
m2.big:
Some small words change the math.
Underline them and slow down.
m2.defn: Trap words are words like increase, square, additional, not, at least that change which calculation you do.
m2.sat: the trap answer is the number you get if you skip the trap word.
m2.hook: Trap words are potholes. Spot them before you drive over them.
how: Underline every trap word.
Write what it means on paper.
Then solve.
m2.rem: Percent increase = change ÷ old. Square units ÷ 144. Bigger sample = smaller margin of error. Don't divide by the new number. Don't divide area by 12.

ex.s: A price rose from $40 to $50. What is the percent increase?
ex.why: Always divide by the old number.
ex.trap: 20%: Divided by the new price. 10 ÷ 50 = 20%. Percent change is measured from the starting value.

ex.s: A value grows from t to 3.47t. By what percent did it increase?
ex.why: The total is 347%, but 100% of that was already there.
ex.trap: 347%: Gave the total. 3.47t is 347% of t, not 347% more. Increase means the extra part only.

ex.s: A floor is 1,584 square inches. How many square feet is it?
ex.why: Square units square the conversion number.
ex.trap: 132: Divided by 12. 1,584 ÷ 12 = 132. 12 converts inches to feet, not square inches to square feet.

ex.s: A plan costs $30 for the first GB and $8 for each additional GB. What does 5 GB cost?
ex.why: The first GB is already in the $30.
ex.trap: $70: Charged $8 for all 5. 30 + 8 × 5 = 70. The first GB was counted twice.

ex.s: A survey of 500 voters has a 4% margin of error. A survey of 2,000 voters will most likely have a margin of error that is…
ex.why: Larger random samples give better estimates.
ex.trap: larger: Went backwards. More data makes an estimate less uncertain. Backwards.

m3.title: Input: put it in Desmos
m3.big:
Don’t solve in your head. Type it into Desmos.
Let the graph show you the answer.
m3.defn: Desmos is the graphing calculator built into the SAT. It can solve equations, find zeros, and find the vertex of a graph.
m3.sat: if you can type the equation, type it. It is faster and you won’t make arithmetic slips.
m3.hook: Desmos is your calculator superpower. Use it on every equation.
how: Type the equation exactly.
Click the point you need (vertex, crossing).
Read the x or y the question asks for.
m3.rem: Desmos finds equation answers, the vertex, and where a graph crosses the x-axis. Don't do it in your head.

ex.trap: 22: Solved in his head. 0.9 + 4.4 = 5.3, but 0.17 × 31 = 5.27. Mental-math slip. Desmos avoids it.

ex.s: y = x² − 8.5x + 20. At what x is y smallest?
ex.trap: 5: Guessed a whole number. The vertex is at 4.25. The low point isn’t always a whole number.

ex.s: What are the zeros of y = x² − x − 12?
ex.trap: 3 and −4: Flipped the signs. Plug in 3: 9 − 3 − 12 = −6, not 0. Signs are flipped.

ex.s: A parabola has zeros at 2 and 10. What is the x-value of the vertex?
ex.why: A parabola is symmetric, so the vertex is in the middle.
ex.trap: 8: Subtracted the zeros. 10 − 2 = 8 is the distance, not the middle. Average them instead.

ex.s: f(x) = 2x² + 3x − 4. What is a + b + c?
ex.why: Plugging in 1 adds up all the coefficients.
ex.trap: 9: Ignored the minus sign. 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. c is −4, not 4.

m4.title: Verify and check edge numbers
m4.big:
Plug your answer back in before you click.
At an edge number, test the edge itself.
m4.defn: Verifying means putting your answer back into the original problem to make sure it works. An edge number is the boundary in an inequality (like −30 in k < −30).
m4.sat: two choices often look right. Plugging in decides between them in seconds.
m4.hook: Check your work before you hand it in.
how: Plug the answer into the original.
At an edge number, ask: "Does this number itself work?"
Systems: simplify both equations and compare.
m4.rem: Plug your answer back in. Test the edge number itself. With < or >, the edge number doesn't count.

ex.s: Which line has slope −½ and passes through (4, 1)?
ex.why: Only this one gives y = 1 at x = 4.
ex.trap: y = −½x + 1: Picked the right slope, wrong intercept. −½(4) + 1 = −1, not 1. The point is not on that line.

ex.s: 3k + 90 < 0. What is the greatest possible integer k?
ex.why: −30 makes it equal 0, which is not less than 0.
ex.trap: −30: Used the edge. 3(−30) + 90 = 0. Is 0 < 0? No. The edge doesn’t work, so step one past it.

ex.s: 2(x + 3) = 2x + k has no solution. Which could be k?
ex.why: Same x-part, different constant → no solution.
ex.trap: 6: Made both sides identical. 2x + 6 = 2x + 6 is always true. That gives infinitely many solutions, not none.

m5.title: Every minute: use the whole clock
m5.big:
Use every minute.
Finished early means you skipped the checking.
m5.defn: Pacing: Math is 35 minutes for 22 questions (about 1½ minutes each). Reading and Writing is 32 minutes for 27 (about 1 minute 10 seconds each). There is no penalty for guessing.
m5.sat: in Practice Test 2 you finished Math Module 2 in 15 minutes and missed 9 Easy questions. That time should have been checking time.
m5.hook: A road trip uses the whole tank: don't park with gas left.
how: Glance at the clock every 5 questions.
Never leave a blank.
Time left at the end = checking time.
m5.rem: About 1½ minutes per math question. Extra time = go back and verify. Never leave a blank. Finishing early means you rushed.

ex.s: 10 minutes are left and every question is answered.
ex.why: Extra time is checking time. That is where easy points come back.
parts: run V: plug answers back in
ex.trap: submit early: Turns in with time left. Practice Test 2: 20 minutes left, 13 wrong. The checking would have caught the easy misses.

ex.s: A question has taken 3 minutes and you are stuck.
ex.why: No penalty for guessing. Spend the time where you can score.
ex.trap: keep working: Stays on one question. 6 min 52 sec on one question (Nov 6). That time could have answered 3 other questions.

ex.s: Time is almost up and two questions are blank.
ex.why: A blank is always wrong; a guess might be right.
ex.trap: leave blank: Skips them. Blank = 0% chance. Guess = 25%. Free points left on the table.

t1.title: Lines, slopes, tables and how many solutions
t1.big:
A line has a slope (how steep) and an intercept (where it crosses).
Most line questions are about one of those two.
t1.defn: Slope = change in y ÷ change in x. In y = mx + b, m is the slope and b is the y-intercept. In Ax + By = C, the slope is −A ÷ B.
t1.sat: decide whether the question wants a slope, an intercept, or a number of solutions.
t1.hook: Perpendicular = flip and switch: flip the fraction, switch the sign.
how: Get the slope (−A ÷ B or from two points).
Perpendicular? Flip and switch.
Intercepts: plug in 0 for the other letter.
t1.rem: Perpendicular: flip and switch. Different x-numbers: one. Same x, different constants: none. All the same: infinitely many. Switching the sign alone is wrong.

ex.s: What is the slope of 3x + 4y = 12?
ex.why: Solve for y; the number on x is the slope.
ex.trap: ¾: Dropped the minus. y = −¾x + 3. Moving 3x across makes it negative.

ex.s: A line has slope −4. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
ex.why: Check: −4 × ¼ = −1 ✓. Perpendicular slopes multiply to −1.
ex.trap: 4: Switched the sign only. −4 × 4 = −16, not −1. You must flip and switch.

ex.s: Where does y = 7x + 14 cross the x-axis?
ex.trap: 2: Sign slip. 7(2) + 14 = 28, not 0. Moving 14 across makes it negative.

ex.s: A line passes through (1, 5) and (3, 11). What is its slope?
ex.why: Rise over run.
ex.trap: 2: Gave the change in x. Δx = 2 is the run only. Slope is rise ÷ run.

ex.s: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6. How many solutions?
ex.why: Both sides are the same line.
ex.trap: one: Assumed one answer. Any x works, e.g. x = 0 and x = 5. Identical sides → infinitely many.

t2.title: Exponents and equivalent expressions
t2.big:
Linear adds the same amount each step.
Exponential multiplies by the same number each step.
t2.defn: In a · bˣ, a is the start and b is the growth factor. b > 1 grows; b < 1 shrinks. In a · 2^(t/k), it doubles every k.
t2.sat: look at the base b first. It tells you grow or shrink, and by how much.
t2.hook: Linear adds the same amount each step. Exponential multiplies.
how: Exponential? Find the base and the number under t.
Table? Divide neighbors, then subtract neighbors.
Expression? Factor the repeated chunk.
t2.rem: Divide neighbors: same ratio = exponential. Subtract: same difference = linear. a·2^(t/k) doubles every k. Don't double the k.

ex.s: f(x) = 500(0.85)ˣ. By what percent does it change each step?
ex.why: Keeps 85%, so it loses 15%.
ex.trap: decreases 85%: Read the base as the loss. 0.85 means 85% remains. The loss is what’s gone: 15%.

ex.s: P = 300 · 2^(t/4). How often does P double?
ex.why: When t goes up by 4, the exponent goes up by 1, so it doubles.
ex.trap: 8: Doubled k. At t = 8, it has doubled twice. One doubling happens every 4.

ex.s: Values: 3, 6, 12, 24. Linear or exponential?
ex.why: Multiplying by 2 each time.
ex.trap: linear: Looked at differences. Differences: 3, 6, 12. Not the same. Not the same amount added.

ex.s: Which is equivalent to 6x² + 9x?
ex.why: Check: 3x · 2x + 3x · 3 = 6x² + 9x ✓.
ex.trap: 3x(2x + 9): Didn’t divide 9x. 3x · 9 = 27x. Each term must be divided by 3x.

ex.s: Simplify (x³)².
ex.why: (x³)² = x³ · x³ = x⁶.
ex.trap: x⁵: Added the exponents. x³ · x³ = x⁶. Adding is for multiplying two powers, not a power of a power.

t3.title: Circles, volume and trig
t3.big:
Most of these use one formula from the reference sheet.
Find the formula, find the radius, plug in.
t3.defn: Circle: d = 2r, A = πr², C = 2πr. Cone volume = ⅓πr²h. In a right triangle, sin of one acute angle = cos of the other. Radians to degrees: replace π with 180°.
t3.sat: the reference sheet at the start of each Math module has these formulas. Use it.
t3.hook: Area squares the change: double a room's width and length and you need 4× the carpet.
how: Write the formula from the reference sheet.
Plug in. Watch the ⅓.
Check the FIND: r or d? degrees?
t3.rem: d = 2r, A = πr², C = πd. Double r = 4× area. Cone = ⅓ × base × h. sin of one acute angle = cos of the other. Don't forget the ⅓. Don't mix up radius and diameter.

ex.s: A circle has area 36π. What is its circumference?
ex.why: Area gives r; then use the circumference formula.
ex.trap: 6π: Used πr instead of 2πr. C = 2πr = 12π. Forgot the 2.

ex.s: A circle’s radius is tripled. Its area is multiplied by…
ex.why: Area uses r², so the scale gets squared.
ex.trap: 3: Didn’t square. π(3r)² = 9πr². Area squares the change.

ex.s: A cone has r = 3 and h = 8. What is its volume?
ex.why: Don’t forget the ⅓.
ex.trap: 72π: Forgot ⅓. That’s a cylinder’s volume. A cone is ⅓ of a cylinder.

ex.t: sin = cos of the other angle
ex.s: In a right triangle, sin A = 0.6. What is cos B (the other acute angle)?
ex.why: The side opposite A is next to B.
ex.trap: 0.8: Found cos A. cos A = 0.8 in a 3-4-5 triangle. The question asks cos B.

ex.s: Convert 2π/3 radians to degrees.
ex.why: π radians = 180°.
ex.trap: 60°: Dropped the 2. 180 ÷ 3 = 60. It is 2π/3, not π/3.

g1.title: Modifiers: the doer goes right after the comma
g1.big:
When a sentence opens with a describing phrase and a comma,
the word right after the comma must be the one doing it.
g1.defn: A modifier is a phrase that describes something. An opening modifier describes whatever comes right after its comma. If the wrong word is there, the modifier is dangling.
g1.sat: the 4 choices start with different words. Ask: who is doing the opening action? That word must come right after the comma.
g1.hook: The opening phrase is a name tag: it must be pinned on the word right after the comma.
how: Read the opening phrase. Ask: who or what is doing it?
Look right after the comma.
Pick the choice that puts that doer first.
g1.rem: Whoever does the opening action goes right after the comma.

ex.s: Studying the night sky, [[Maria Mitchell]] spotted a new comet.
ex.why: Mitchell is the one studying, so she goes right after the comma.
ex.trap: a new comet was spotted: Puts “a new comet” after the comma. Studying the night sky, a new comet was spotted… Now the comet is studying the sky. Comets can’t study.

ex.s: Built in 1884, [[the Washington Monument]] was once the world’s tallest structure.
ex.why: The monument was built, so it goes right after the comma.
ex.trap: visitors climb: Puts “visitors” after the comma. Built in 1884, visitors climb… The visitors weren’t built in 1884.

ex.s: After pleading for years, [[the activists]] staged a sit-in protest.
ex.why: The activists did the pleading. (Based on a real College Board question.)
ex.trap: pressure on lawmakers increased: Puts “pressure” after the comma. After pleading for years, pressure on lawmakers increased… Pressure can’t plead.

ex.s: As a young writer, [[Eudora Welty]] worked as a photographer.
ex.why: Welty was the young writer.
ex.trap: a government agency hired: Puts the agency after the comma. As a young writer, a government agency hired Welty. The agency was not a young writer.

ex.s: To test the theory, [[the researchers]] built a model.
ex.why: The researchers are doing the testing.
ex.trap: a model was built: Puts “a model” after the comma. To test the theory, a model was built. A model can’t test a theory by itself.

ex.s: Hiking through the Andes, [[the botanist]] found a rare orchid.
ex.why: The botanist was hiking.
ex.trap: the botanist’s notebook: Uses an ’s word. Hiking through the Andes, the botanist’s notebook filled up… With ’s, the subject becomes the notebook. Notebooks don’t hike.

g2.title: Lists and pairs must match
g2.big: Every item in a list or pair must have the same form.
g2.defn: Parallel structure means items joined by and, or, both…and, not only…but also, or either…or match in form: all -ing, all plain verbs, all nouns, or all describing words.
g2.sat: find the other items in the list. Look at their form. Make the blank match.
g2.hook: Items in a list are matching socks in a drawer: same kind, same form.
how: Find the list or pair.
Look at the form of the first item.
Make the blank match it.
g2.rem: Every item in a list or pair has the same form.

ex.s: The researchers spent their days measuring, photographing, and [[sampling]] the coral.
ex.why: The first two are -ing, so the third is too.
ex.trap: to sample: Switches to “to + verb.” measuring, photographing, and to sample Doesn’t match the -ing items.

ex.s: The guide told the hikers to stretch, [[drink]] water, and rest.
ex.why: “To” is shared: to stretch, (to) drink, (to) rest.
ex.trap: drinking: Uses -ing. to stretch, drinking water, and rest Stretch and rest are plain verbs. -ing breaks the pattern.

ex.s: The experiment needed soil, seeds, and [[a light source]].
ex.why: Three things.
ex.trap: lighting the plants: Switches to an action. soil, seeds, and lighting the plants An action in a list of things.

ex.s: The new library is not only larger but also [[quieter]].
ex.why: Larger / quieter: both describing words.
ex.trap: it is quieter: Adds a whole new sentence part. not only larger but also it is quieter Doesn’t match “larger.”

g3.title: Verb tense and form
g3.big:
Verb tense tells you when something happened.
Find the time clue, then match the verb.
g3.defn: Tense is the form of a verb that shows time: past (found), present (finds), has/have + verb (has found: from then until now), had + verb (had found: before another past event).
g3.sat: circle the time clue (a date, “since,” “by the time,” or the tense of the other verbs). Pick the tense that matches.
g3.hook: Read the time stamp: when is this sentence happening?
how: Find the time clue (a date, since, by the time, now).
Find the who (one or many).
Pick the verb that matches both.
g3.rem: 1969 → past. Since → has/have. By the time (past) → had.

ex.s: In 1969, astronauts [[landed]] on the moon.
ex.why: A finished past event → simple past.
ex.trap: land: Uses present. In 1969, astronauts land… 1969 is over.

ex.s: Since 2020, the museum [[has won]] three awards.
ex.why: “Since” stretches to now → has won.
ex.trap: won: Uses plain past. Since 2020, the museum won… Plain past doesn’t reach up to now.

ex.s: By the time the rescue team arrived, the storm [[had ended]].
ex.why: The storm ended before the team arrived → had ended.
ex.trap: has ended: Uses has. the storm has ended “Has” reaches to now, but this is all in the past.

ex.t: In the middle of it → was / were + -ing
ex.s: Bonnie Buratti [[was studying]] Saturn’s rings when she made a discovery.
ex.why: She was in the middle of studying when the discovery happened. (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: studies: Uses present. Buratti studies… when she made… “Made” is past, so the verb must be past.

ex.s: Economists in India use an index. This tool [[measures]] quality of life.
ex.why: A general fact, matching the present “use.” (Real College Board question.)
ex.trap: had measured: Uses had. This tool had measured… Nothing here is before another past event.

a1.title: Quadratics: zeros, vertex, how many solutions
a1.big:
A quadratic has an x². Its graph is a U-shape (parabola).
Each form shows you something different.
a1.defn: Standard ax² + bx + c (c = y-intercept) · Factored a(x − p)(x − q) (zeros p and q) · Vertex a(x − h)² + k (vertex (h, k)). Discriminant b² − 4ac: positive → 2 solutions, 0 → 1, negative → 0.
a1.sat: match the question to the form: zeros → factored, vertex → vertex form, y-intercept → standard. Or graph it in Desmos.
a1.hook: The discriminant is a traffic light: positive = 2 answers, zero = 1, negative = 0.
how: Name the form.
What does the question want: zeros, vertex, or how many solutions?
Use the matching tool (factor, read the form, or b² − 4ac).
a1.rem: Standard shows the y-intercept, factored shows the zeros, vertex form shows the vertex. b² − 4ac counts the solutions.

ex.s: y = 2(x − 3)(x + 5). Zeros?
ex.why: The zero has the opposite sign of the number in the factor.
ex.trap: −3, 5: Copied the signs. Plug in −3: (−6)(2) ≠ 0. Signs flip.

ex.s: y = (x − 4)² + 7. Vertex?
ex.why: Inside the parentheses the sign flips; outside it doesn’t.
ex.trap: (−4, 7): Copied the sign. At x = −4: 64 + 7 = 71, not the minimum. h = +4.

ex.s: y = x² − 6x + 8. y-intercept?
ex.why: At x = 0 every x-term vanishes.
ex.trap: −6: Used b. b is the x-coefficient. Only c is left at x = 0.

ex.s: y = 2x² − 12x + 1. x of the vertex?
ex.why: The vertex is on the axis of symmetry.
ex.trap: −3: Sign slip. −b = −(−12) = +12. Double negative.

ex.s: How many real solutions does x² + 4x + 5 = 0 have?
ex.why: Negative discriminant → the graph never touches the x-axis.
ex.trap: 2: Assumed a quadratic always has 2. Desmos: the graph stays above the x-axis. Negative → no real solutions.

a2.title: Systems: words to equations, then solve
a2.big:
A system is two equations with two unknowns.
Turn each sentence into one equation, then solve.
a2.defn: A system of equations is solved by the pair of values that makes both equations true. On a graph, that is where the two lines cross.
a2.sat: one equation usually counts how many, and the other counts how much (money, weight).
a2.hook: Two equations, two unknowns: like two refs agreeing on one call.
how: Write FIND and name each letter.
One sentence → one equation. Check who is bigger.
Solve (substitute, eliminate, or Desmos), then plug back in.
a2.rem: The bigger one equals 4 times the smaller: A = 4B.

ex.s: Adult $12, child $8. 20 tickets, $200. Adult tickets?
ex.why: Check: 10 adults + 10 kids = $120 + $80 = $200 ✓.
ex.trap: 5: Guessed. 5 adults + 15 kids = $60 + $120 = $180. Doesn’t make $200.

ex.s: There are 4 times as many blue marbles as red. There are 35 in all. How many blue?
ex.trap: 7: Gave red. 7 is the red count. The FIND is blue.

ex.s: x + y = 10 and x − y = 4. Find x.
ex.why: Adding cancels y.
ex.trap: 3: Gave y. y = 3, x = 7. The FIND is x.

a3.title: Functions and rearranging formulas
a3.big:
A function is a machine: put x in, get f(x) out.
f(3) means put 3 in. f(x) = 7 means the output is 7.
a3.defn: In f(x) = 3x − 5, x is the input and f(x) is the output. f(0) is the y-intercept. To rearrange a formula, undo + and − first, then × and ÷.
a3.sat: ask: am I given the input (plug in) or the output (solve)?
a3.hook: Rearranging = unpacking a gear bag: last thing packed comes out first.
how: Circle the letter you need alone.
Undo + and − first.
Then undo × and ÷. Check with a quick number.
a3.rem: Undo plus and minus first, then times and divide. Check with a number.

ex.why: Exponents before multiplying.
ex.trap: 35: Multiplied before squaring. (2 · 3)² − 1 = 35. Only x is squared, not 2x.

ex.s: f(x) = 3x − 5. For what x is f(x) = 7?
ex.why: The 7 is the output, so solve for x.
ex.trap: 16: Plugged 7 in as x. f(7) = 16, but the question says f(x) = 7. Input and output mixed up.

ex.s: g(x) = ax + 2 and g(5) = 37. What is a?
ex.why: A point gives one equation for the missing number.
ex.trap: 35: Stopped early. 5a = 35, so a = 7. Divide by 5.

ex.s: A = ½bh. Solve for h.
ex.why: Multiply by 2, then divide by b.
ex.trap: A ÷ 2b: Divided by 2 instead of multiplying. Check A = ½ · b · (A/2b) = A/4. Doesn’t return A.

ex.s: How is y = f(x − 3) moved from y = f(x)?
ex.why: Inside the parentheses, the direction is the opposite of the sign.
ex.trap: 3 left: Followed the minus sign. f(x − 3) reaches the old f(0) at x = 3. It moved right.

a4.title: Absolute value
a4.big:
|x| is the distance from 0.
Distance is never negative, and you can go either way.
a4.defn: The absolute value of a number is its distance from 0. |5| = 5 and |−5| = 5. So |x − a| = b means x is b away from a, in either direction.
a4.sat: always write two equations. The trap is giving only one answer.
a4.hook: Absolute value is distance from home: you can be on either side of it.
how: Get the absolute value alone.
Negative on the other side? No solution.
Otherwise split into + and − and solve both.
a4.rem: Absolute value is distance: 5 above 3 and 5 below 3, so 8 and −2.

ex.why: Both are 5 away from 3.
ex.trap: 8 only: Wrote one equation. |−2 − 3| = |−5| = 5 ✓ too. Missed the other side.

ex.why: An absolute value is never negative.
ex.trap: x = −6: Solved anyway. |−6 + 4| = 2, not −2. Doesn’t check.

ex.why: Only one number is 0 away from 5.
ex.trap: 5 and −5: Made two answers. |−5 − 5| = 10. Zero has only one side.

ex.s: A temperature t stays within 2 degrees of 70. Inequality?
ex.why: “Within” means at most that far.
ex.trap: |t − 70| ≥ 2: Flipped the sign. t = 80 would fit, but it’s 10 away. ≥ means at least 2 away.

a5.title: Inequalities from words and graphs
a5.big:
An inequality is like an equation, but with <, >, ≤, ≥.
Flip the sign when you multiply or divide by a negative.
a5.defn: at least ≥ · at most / no more than ≤ · more than > · fewer / less than <. Dividing both sides by a negative reverses the sign.
a5.sat: circle any negative you divide by, and the trap words at least / at most.
a5.hook: At least = "or more," like "at least 16 years old" to drive.
how: Translate each phrase into a symbol.
Solve. Divided by a negative? Flip.
Test one number to check.
a5.rem: At least ≥, at most ≤, no more than ≤. Flip when multiplying or dividing by a negative.

ex.s: You must be at least 16 to drive. Age a?
ex.why: 16 itself counts.
ex.trap: a > 16: Left out 16. A 16-year-old can drive. “At least” includes the number.
x > −4: Didn’t flip. x = 0: 0 > 8? No. Must flip when dividing by a negative.

ex.s: Is (1, 4) a solution of y > 2x + 1?
ex.why: Plug in and check.
ex.trap: no: Guessed from the graph. 4 > 3 is true. Always plug in.

ex.s: In 12x + 19y ≤ 300, what does 19y mean?
ex.why: Each term is a price times a count.
ex.trap: number of y items: Read only y. 19y is dollars, not a count. y alone is the count.

a6.title: Ratios, rates and unit conversions
a6.big:
A ratio or rate compares two amounts.
Line up the units and let them cancel.
a6.defn: A rate is an amount per one unit (miles per hour). A proportion sets two ratios equal. To convert units, multiply by fractions equal to 1 so the units cancel.
a6.sat: write the units next to every number. Wrong units = wrong answer.
a6.hook: Units are puzzle pieces: match them top and bottom, and the ones that match cancel out.
how: Write the units next to every number.
Line up matching units (or change to per 1).
Multiply or divide, and check that the units left are the FIND.
a6.rem: Same units on top, same units on the bottom, then cross-multiply.

ex.s: 3 cups for 4 servings. Cups for 10?
ex.why: Same units on top and bottom of both fractions.
ex.trap: 13.3: Flipped one fraction. 3/4 = 10/c gives c ≈ 13.3. Cups ended up on the bottom.

ex.s: 60 miles per hour = how many feet per second?
ex.why: Miles → feet (× 5,280), hours → seconds (÷ 3,600).
ex.trap: 1: Converted only hours. 60 ÷ 60 = 1 mile per minute. Still in miles, not feet per second.

ex.s: Split 40 in the ratio 3:5.
ex.trap: 3 and 5: Used the ratio numbers. 3 + 5 = 8, not 40. Those are parts, not amounts.

ex.s: A car goes 45 mph for 2.5 hours. Distance?
ex.why: Units: miles/hour × hours = miles.
ex.trap: 18: Divided. 45 ÷ 2.5 = 18. Distance multiplies.

d1.title: Mean, median and spread
d1.big:
Mean = the average. Median = the middle.
Spread = how far apart the values are.
d1.defn: Mean = sum ÷ count. Median = middle value in order (average the two middles if even). Range = max − min. Standard deviation = typical distance from the mean.
d1.sat: outlier questions ask which changes more, the mean or the median.
d1.hook: Mean is the class average. Median is the middle student in line.
how: Put the numbers in order.
Mean: add and divide. Median: find the middle.
Spread: which set is more stretched out?
d1.rem: It pulls the mean a lot and barely moves the median.

ex.why: Put the numbers in order before finding the middle.
ex.trap: median 11: Took the middle of the unsorted list. In order: 4, 8, 9, 11, 18. Must sort first.

ex.s: Add 100 to the list 4, 8, 9, 11, 18. Which changes more?
ex.why: The mean uses every value’s size; the median only its position.
ex.trap: the median: Assumed both change equally. Median moved 1; mean moved 15. The mean is pulled by extremes.

ex.t: Add the same to every value
ex.s: Add 5 to every value. What happens to the spread?
ex.why: Mean and median go up 5; range and SD stay.
ex.trap: increases by 5: Moved the spread too. Range: (18 + 5) − (4 + 5) = 14, same. Shifting doesn’t spread values apart.

ex.s: The mean of 4 tests is 85. After a 5th test, it is 86. What was the 5th score?
ex.why: Work with totals, not averages.
ex.trap: 86: Gave the new mean. (340 + 86) ÷ 5 = 85.2. Doesn’t make the mean 86.

d2.title: Probability and two-way tables
d2.big:
Probability = favorable ÷ total.
“Given that” shrinks the total to one row or column.
d2.defn: The probability of an event is (number of favorable outcomes) ÷ (total outcomes). In a two-way table, “given that,” “of those who,” or “among” means the total is just that row or column. Expected number = probability × how many.
d2.sat: circle “given that.” It tells you which number goes on the bottom.
d2.hook: "Given that" = zoom in on one row or column, like zooming in on one row of a spreadsheet.
how: Find the group they're talking about (the "given").
Its total goes on the bottom.
The matching cell goes on top.
d2.rem: It shrinks the total to just that row or column.

ex.s: 4 red, 6 blue, 10 green. P(blue)?
ex.why: Bottom = all marbles.
ex.trap: 6/14: Left blue out of the total. Total must include blue. Bottom is all 20.

ex.s: Grade 10: 30 play a sport, 20 don’t. Grade 11: 15 play, 35 don’t. Given a student doesn’t play, P(grade 10)?
ex.why: Zoom in on the “doesn’t play” group.
ex.trap: 20/100: Used the whole table. The question limits it to non-players. Wrong bottom number.

ex.s: A part is defective with probability 0.02. About how many of 1,500 are defective?
ex.why: Multiply the chance by the count.

d3.title: Scatterplots, models and residuals
d3.big:
A line of best fit predicts y from x.
Slope = change per 1 more x. Intercept = y when x is 0.
d3.defn: In a model y = mx + b: m is the predicted change in y for each 1-unit increase in x, and b is the predicted y when x = 0. A residual is actual − predicted.
d3.sat: say the slope as a sentence with both units: “for each 1 more , y goes up .”
d3.hook: Slope is miles per hour: how much y changes for each 1 of x.
how: Name what x and y stand for.
Slope = change per 1 x; intercept = at x = 0.
Same amount → linear. Same percent → exponential.
d3.rem: Slope: change in y for each 1 more x. Intercept: y when x is 0.

ex.s: y = 2.5x + 40. What does 2.5 mean?
ex.why: Change in y for each 1 more x.
ex.trap: score with 0 hours: Described the intercept. That’s 40. Slope is a rate, not a starting value.

ex.s: y = 2.5x + 40. What does 40 mean?
ex.why: The start value.
ex.trap: points per hour: Described the slope. That’s 2.5. Intercept is where x = 0.

ex.s: y = 2.5x + 40. Predict y for 6 hours.
ex.why: Use the model.
ex.trap: 15: Forgot the intercept. 2.5 × 6 alone. Add 40.

ex.s: A student studied 6 hours and scored 60. Residual?
ex.why: Positive: the point is above the line.
ex.trap: −5: Subtracted backwards. predicted − actual = −5. Residual is actual − predicted.

ex.s: y = 3ˣ vs. y = 4x + 1 for x > 0. Which is true?
ex.why: Exponential growth always wins in the long run.
ex.trap: the exponential is always greater: Ignored small x. At x = 1, 3 < 5. “Always” is too strong.

e1.title: Similar shapes: sides, perimeter, area, volume
e1.big:
Similar shapes have the same shape, different size.
Every side is multiplied by the same scale factor k.
e1.defn: Two shapes are similar if all matching angles are equal and all matching sides are in the same ratio, k. Perimeter × k, area × k², volume × k³.
e1.sat: ask: sides, area, or volume? That tells you k, k², or k³.
e1.hook: Zoom a photo 2×: each side doubles, but the picture takes up 4× the space.
how: Find k (big side ÷ small side, or √ of the area ratio).
Length or perimeter → × k. Area → × k². Volume → × k³.
Check: does the big shape get the big number?
e1.rem: Perimeter × k, area × k², volume × k³.

ex.s: A 3-4-5 triangle is scaled by 2. New sides?
ex.why: Every side uses the same k.
ex.trap: 5, 6, 7: Added 2. 3 + 2 = 5. Similar means multiply, not add.

ex.s: Area 10, scaled by 3. New area?
ex.why: Area has two dimensions, so square k.
ex.trap: 30: Used k. 10 × 3 = 30. Area changes by k².

ex.s: A box is scaled by 2. Its volume is multiplied by…
ex.why: Three dimensions → cube k.
ex.trap: 4: Used k². 2² = 4 is for area. Volume uses k³.

ex.s: Two similar shapes have areas 25 and 9. Ratio of their sides?
ex.why: Undo the square.
ex.trap: 25 : 9: Used the area ratio. Sides 25:9 would make areas 625:81. Take the square root.

e2.title: Angles, triangles and parallel lines
e2.big:
A straight line is 180°. A triangle adds to 180°.
Parallel lines repeat the same angles at each crossing.
e2.defn: Angles on a straight line add to 180°. Triangle angles add to 180°. Vertical (crossing) angles are equal. With parallel lines cut by a transversal, all acute angles are equal, all obtuse angles are equal, and acute + obtuse = 180°.
e2.sat: mark every angle you know on the figure, then use 180.
e2.hook: Parallel lines are railroad tracks: the same angles repeat at each crossing.
how: Label every angle you know on paper.
Use 180 (triangle or line), equal (vertical or parallel), or 90 (right triangle).
Write an equation and solve.
e2.rem: Acute angles are equal, obtuse angles are equal, and acute + obtuse = 180.

ex.s: Angles 50° and 60°. Third?
ex.why: Triangles always total 180°.
ex.trap: 110°: Stopped at the sum. 50 + 60 + 110 = 220. Too big.

ex.s: Two angles on a line; one is 130°. The other?
ex.why: A straight line is 180°.
ex.trap: 130°: Assumed equal. 130 + 130 = 260. Only vertical angles are equal.

ex.s: Two lines cross. One angle is 40°. The angle opposite it?
ex.why: Opposite angles at a crossing match.
ex.trap: 140°: Used the angle beside it. 140° is next to it, not opposite. Opposite = equal.

ex.s: Parallel lines are cut by a transversal. One acute angle is 65°. An obtuse angle?
ex.why: Every acute angle is 65°, every obtuse angle is 115°.
ex.trap: 65°: Picked the acute size. Obtuse angles are bigger than 90°. 65° is acute.

ex.s: A right triangle has a 35° angle. The other acute angle?
ex.why: The right angle uses 90 of the 180.
